excerpt: Once installed, cubic automatically reviews new pull requests.
To review a PR that was opened _before_ you installed the app, comment: `@cubic-dev-ai review this PR`.
Ultrareview runs a longer review using cubic's most capable review models, which is useful for risky migrations, security-sensitive changes, or complex refactors.
cubic generates the fix and pushes it to your PR branch.
Reply to a review comment to ask for clarification:
Enable [auto-approval](/ai-review/auto-approval) to let cubic approve PRs that meet your review policy.
The **cubic CLI** reviews local changes before you push. It finds bugs and generates a prompt that your coding agent can use to fix them.
Connect cubic's MCP server to your coding agent to read review findings and codebase context, request PR reviews, and triage PR or codebase scan issues.
Custom agents are review rules that enforce your organization's specific best practices across pull requests.
cubic automatically learns when you: Reply to its comments... React to suggestions: Thumbs up/down help cubic calibrate what's useful vs noise
`cubic.yaml` lives in the root of your repository and becomes the source of truth for AI review behavior, ignore patterns, PR descriptions, and custom agents.
Codebase scans deploy thousands of AI agents to find bugs and vulnerabilities across your repository.
cubic's AI wiki automatically indexes your codebase and produces searchable wikis, complete with links to source code, architecture diagrams, and more.
Focus on implementation changes by hiding test files from the PR diff and file tree.
You can now ask your coding agent to check your cubic subscription, manage team seats and roles, and purchase more seats without leaving your MCP client.
The Analytics API gives you PR-level data on how many issues were flagged, how many were fixed, how much AI code was authored, etc.
cubic skills give your coding agent instructions for reviewing code, handling PR comments, and using your team's codebase context.
7 days free, no credit card required.

I really liked it - it hit the mark. The current balance works very well, and it genuinely surprised me. It provides more technical explanations than just basic checks; for example, compared to using a regular GPT or Claude. I may not be an experienced developer, but I can confidently say that your Cubic.dev is really powerful.

The 'in-codebase' approach is the right one, but a YAML file with plain text is a half-measure. The most reliable rule that 'lives next to the code' is an architectural test... a more robust engineering solution, unlike semantic text interpretation, which can fail.
